title: Learning Efficient Draft Blocks for Speculative Decoding
area: ML Systems & Efficient ML / Speculative Decoding
question: Design the head that reads L future positions from a single drafter forward so accepted tokens per target forward go up.
elab:
A frozen autoregressive drafter supplies context features; a learned block head proposes several future tokens from one drafter forward. The task improves accepted tokens per target-model verification, including a setting that prices verification cost.

Speculative decoding proposes tokens cheaply and verifies them with one parallel forward of the target model; the cheapest proposer runs the drafter once and reads a whole block of future positions off that single forward. Medusa, DFlash and their successors are different designs for the head that does that reading. The task fixes a Qwen2.5-7B-Instruct target, a frozen small drafter and the verifier and asks for the block head, measured by accepted tokens per target forward when the target's own answers to MT-Bench, GSM8K and HumanEval are decoded round by round. It matters because the head is the only part of the system that is cheap to change and it sets the speed-up directly.

description_md:
# Parallel Block Heads for Speculative Decoding

## Research Question

Speculative decoding accelerates autoregressive generation by proposing tokens
cheaply and checking them with one parallel forward of the large *target* model.
The cheapest proposer imaginable runs the small *drafter* **once** and reads a
whole block of `L` future positions off that single forward.

The difficulty is that an ordinary autoregressive drafter has nothing to say
about position 2 from one forward: position 2's distribution is conditioned on
position 1's token, and no token has been chosen yet. Measured on a small-model
pilot of this harness, the probability that the target's token at block position
`j` is among the drafter's top-8 candidates is **0.96 at `j = 1` and 0.01 at
`j = 2`** — from the second position on, an untrained parallel proposal is at
chance.

So a parallel block is not something a drafter *has*; it is something a **block
head** must be built and trained to produce. Given a frozen drafter backbone and
one forward of it, **what block head — architecture and training objective —
makes the `L` emitted positions carry more than one position's worth of
information?**

## Background

**Medusa** — Cai, Li, Geng, Peng, Lee, Chen, Dao, *Medusa: Simple LLM Inference
Acceleration Framework with Multiple Decoding Heads*, arXiv:2401.10774. Adds
`L - 1` extra decoding heads, each a residual block plus its own output
projection, reading the backbone's last hidden state and predicting one future
offset. The heads are **independent**: nothing in head `k` sees head `k-1`'s
output, so the block carries no intra-block dependency at all. Medusa-1 freezes
the backbone and trains only the heads.

**DFlash** — Chen, Liang, Liu, *DFlash: Block Diffusion for Flash Speculative
Decoding*, arXiv:2602.06036, ICML 2026. Replaces independent heads with a
**block-diffusion** drafter: the whole block is denoised jointly, every position
conditioned on the current state of all the others, so the block acquires
dependency without any position waiting on a choice made downstream.

**DFlash 2** — Inco AI, *DFlash 2: Keep Drafting Parallel*, 2026,
`https://inco.ai/blog/dflash2/`. Two mechanisms: **two-tap depthwise dynamic
convolutions** that mix each block position with its predecessor to fight suffix
decay, and a **learned pairwise path selector** — rather than committing to the
per-position argmax, keep the top candidates at every position and score
*adjacent candidate pairs* with a low-rank bilinear form, then trace the single
best-scoring path through the retained lattice. Its stated motivation is the gap
between the top-1 being right and the truth merely being retained.

> Provenance, stated rather than smoothed over: **DFlash 2 is not a paper.**
> There is no arXiv id and no peer review; it is a vendor blog post with released
> checkpoints. It is a *checkable* reference, and the DFlash repository's own
> README cites it as `@misc{inco2026dflash2}`.

**DSpark** — Cheng, Yu, Shao, Li, Xiong, …, Zhang, Zhao, Liang (DeepSeek-AI and
Peking University), *DSpark: Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with
Semi-Autoregressive Generation*, arXiv:2607.05147. A **sequential Markov head**
injects first-order dependency as a low-rank transition bias on the block logits,
`B(x_{k-1}, ·) = W1[x_{k-1}] W2`, applied position by position to the token
actually chosen at `k-1`; a **confidence head** predicts each position's
conditional acceptance, and the number of positions submitted for verification is
scheduled from the cumulative survival.

## Neighbouring Tasks

The other `spec-*` tasks in this suite take the drafter's proposal as given and
choose what to do with it — which subtree to verify, which candidate to keep, how
much budget to spend. Here the proposal itself is the object: you are building
and training the thing that produces the block. An edit that wins one of those
tasks cannot win this one, and vice versa.

## What You Can Modify

**One file, one class:** `speculative-sampling/mlsb_blockhead.py`, inside the
marked editable region — the body of `CustomBlockHead`. Three methods:

```python
build(cfg)                        -> torch.nn.Module
loss(module, hidden, tokens, aux) -> scalar tensor
propose(module, hidden)           -> (cand_token, cand_logp, n_submit)
```

`build(cfg)` constructs the head, once. `cfg` carries `d_model`, `vocab`,
`block_len` (`L`), `top_k` (`K`), `cost_c`, `device`, the frozen backbone's own
output embedding `lm_head_weight`, and `shared_proj` — an output projection
already initialised from it. Everything the head needs at inference must live
**inside the returned module** (parameters, or `register_buffer` for anything
fitted but not trained), because training and proposing happen in two separate
processes and only the module's `state_dict` travels between them.

`loss(...)` is **the training objective**. `hidden` is `(B, S, d_model)` from the
frozen backbone, detached. `tokens` is `(B, S + L)`: the training stream is the
**target model's own greedy answers** to a set of chat, code and math requests
(self-distillation), so the tokens after a position are the target's greedy
continuation of it. `aux` carries `step`, `total_steps`, `n_micro`, a seeded
`generator` for any randomness your objective needs, and the **target model's
own cached distribution** — `aux["target_top"]` and `aux["target_logp"]`, its
most likely tokens with log-probabilities at every position, teacher-forced.
Distilling from the distribution is what the EAGLE family does; training on
`tokens` is what Medusa does; both are legitimate.

`propose(...)` returns the block from ONE backbone forward. `hidden` is
`(B, d_model)` — one vector per item, the backbone's state at the position a
decoding round starts from, and the entire input, because at inference the
continuation is exactly what is unknown. It is called, in batches on the GPU,
for every position a round could start from. Return `K` candidates per
position with their log-probabilities, best first, and `n_submit ∈ [1, L]`: how
many leading positions you actually submit. Submitting fewer can only lower the
accepted length, and pays off only where `cfg["cost_c"] > 0`.

Unlike the sibling `spec-*` tasks, **one head object persists across every
evaluation item**, because a trained head must. Nothing is fed back between items.

## Fixed Setup

The drafter backbone is **frozen** and identical for every submission; so are the
target model, the verification rule, and all measurement. **The training recipe
is fixed harness code**, not yours to design: the optimiser (AdamW, `lr = 1e-3`,
linear warmup then cosine decay, gradient clipping), the number of steps, the
batch shape, the sequence length and the order the training windows arrive in are
constants shared by every arm. You supply a module and an objective. "Same
training budget" is therefore true by construction rather than by enforcement.

Your code runs in two processes that receive arrays and return a checkpoint and
then candidate indices: no model, no tokenizer, no target, no access to the
measurement, and the target's greedy continuation never exists in either of them.

## Parameter Budget

Your head's **trainable** parameter count may not exceed **1.05× the largest
reference baseline's**, measured at each setting. That bound is set by Medusa's
`L - 1` independent output projections, so it is generous — every other reference
shares one projection across block positions and sits far below it. Parameters
reused across positions (`cfg["shared_proj"]`, or any module you reference more
than once) are counted once. A submission over the cap is rejected before
training, not scored down.

## Metric

**`tau`** — the average number of tokens produced per decoding round, measured
by decoding: the target's own greedy answers to held-out prompts are replayed
round by round. At a round starting at position `t`, let `g_1, g_2, …` be the
target's greedy continuation. The target verifies your submitted block in one
forward and accepts the longest prefix of `g` that your block's top-1 tokens
match; that same forward yields one more token for free, and the next round
starts after it. So

```
tau = (tokens produced) / (rounds),    k = the matching prefix within n_submit per round
```

is the number of tokens decoded per target forward. **Higher is better.** Where
a setting prices verification,

```
eff_tau = (tokens produced) / sum over rounds of (1 + cost_c · n_submit)
```

which is exactly `tau` when `cost_c` is 0. Both are deterministic functions of
your returned blocks and the target's answers. The task score combines several
evaluation prompt sets and settings into one summary value.

Diagnostics reported but **not** scored: the per-position acceptance curve
(`top1_j`, the probability your argmax at position `j` is right, and `topk_j`,
the probability the truth is among your `K` candidates there), `oracle_tau` (what
a perfect selection among the candidates you retained would have scored),
`n_submit` and `trainable_params`.

## Reference Baselines

**Medusa independent heads** — arXiv:2401.10774; `L - 1` residual-block heads,
one per offset, no intra-block dependency, frozen backbone.

**DFlash block diffusion** — arXiv:2602.06036; masked denoising over the whole
block, iterated at inference from a fully masked start.

**DFlash 2 dynamic convolutions + path selector** — `inco.ai/blog/dflash2/`;
two-tap depthwise dynamic mixing between adjacent positions, plus a low-rank
bilinear pairwise selector traced by Viterbi over the retained candidates.

**DSpark Markov bias + confidence schedule** — arXiv:2607.05147; a low-rank
first-order transition bias applied sequentially, with a learned confidence head
scheduling how much of the block to submit.

**Unmodified starter** — no block head at all: position 1 is the backbone's own
next-token distribution and every later position reuses it.

baselines.docstring:
Medusa: independent per-position decoding heads (the NO-DEPENDENCY rung).

Reference: Tianle Cai, Yuhong Li, Zhengyang Geng, Hongwu Peng, Jason D. Lee,
Deming Chen, Tri Dao, "Medusa: Simple LLM Inference Acceleration Framework with
Multiple Decoding Heads", arXiv:2401.10774; released implementation
`FasterDecoding/Medusa`, `medusa/model/medusa_model.py`.

Protocol ported, and it is Medusa-1 exactly:
  * the backbone is FROZEN and only the heads train (Medusa-1, Sec. 3.1);
  * head k is `Linear(d, V, bias=False) o ResBlock`, with
    `ResBlock(x) = x + SiLU(Linear(d, d)(x))`, the Linear ZERO-initialised so the
    block starts as the identity, and the output projection initialised from the
    backbone's own lm_head -- `medusa/model/medusa_model.py`;
  * head k reads the backbone's last hidden state h_t and predicts the token at
    t + k, with NOTHING from head k-1: the heads are independent, which is the
    property this task's other three arms exist to improve on;
  * block position 1 is the backbone's own (frozen) lm_head, unchanged;
  * the loss is Medusa's weighted sum, `sum_k decay^(k-2) * CE`, decay = 0.8.

Named deviation -- ONE, and it is deliberate: **the loss is distilled from the
target's cached teacher-forced top-k rather than from the corpus token labels.**
Medusa as released trains on corpus labels: the vendored copy of its training
loop at `vendor/external_packages/Liger-Kernel/examples/medusa/medusa_util.py:
231-235` is `CrossEntropyLoss(medusa_logits[i, :, :-(1+i)], labels[..., (1+i):])`,
i.e. head `i` against the dataset's own tokens. Medusa's paper also describes a
self-distillation variant for when the original training data is unavailable,
which is the precedent for doing it this way here.

The reason to deviate is attribution, not fidelity for its own sake: if `medusa`
trained on corpus labels while the other three distilled from the target, a
measured difference between them would confound the block-head architecture with
the training signal, and this task's whole claim is that the arms differ only in
the block head. Every arm therefore gets the same signal. The cost of the
deviation is measured rather than assumed -- a `medusa` run on corpus labels is
kept as an unscored diagnostic so the size of the signal effect is on the record.

Everything else ports whole. Its `L - 1` independent output projections are also
what SETS the task's parameter budget -- every other arm shares one projection
across positions and sits far below the cap.

Test: `medusa` must beat `default` (which is this same file with the heads
removed, i.e. position 1's distribution reused at every position) on every
setting. If it does not, the port is wrong (a pre-registered kill condition).

"""Parallel block head for speculative decoding (EDITABLE).

A speculative decoder proposes several tokens per target forward.  The cheapest
possible proposer runs the drafter ONCE and reads a whole block of ``L`` future
positions off that single forward -- but an ordinary autoregressive drafter has
nothing to say about position 2 from one forward, because position 2's
distribution is conditioned on position 1's token, which has not been chosen yet.
Measured on this harness's gpt2 pilot: the probability that the target's token
at position ``j`` is among the drafter's top-8 candidates was **0.96 at j = 1
and 0.01 at j = 2** -- the drafter is at chance from the second position on.

So a parallel block is not something a drafter *has*; it is something a block
head has to be *built and trained* to produce.  That is the question this file
answers, and the released systems answer it differently -- which is the whole
method:

* **Medusa** (arXiv:2401.10774): ``L - 1`` *independent* heads, one per offset,
  each predicting its position from ``h`` alone.  No intra-block dependency.
* **DFlash** (arXiv:2602.06036, ICML 2026): a *block diffusion* objective -- the
  whole block is denoised jointly, each position conditioned on the current
  state of all the others.
* **DFlash 2** (Inco AI, 2026): *local mixing* -- two-tap depthwise dynamic
  convolutions tie each position to its predecessor -- plus a learned pairwise
  **path selector** over the retained top-``K`` candidates.
* **DSpark** (arXiv:2607.05147): an explicit first-order **Markov transition
  bias** on the block logits, plus a **confidence head** predicting how far down
  the block the dependency still holds.

Everything else is fixed by the harness: the frozen drafter backbone, the
optimiser, the learning-rate schedule, the number of steps, the batch shape, the
token stream, the target model and the measurement.  **You design a module and
an objective; you do not design a training recipe.**

Interface contract
------------------
``build(cfg) -> torch.nn.Module``

    Construct and return the head.  Called ONCE, before training.  Everything
    the head needs at inference must live **inside the returned module** --
    parameters, or ``register_buffer`` for anything fitted but not trained --
    because training and proposing happen in two separate processes and only the
    module's ``state_dict`` travels between them.  ``cfg`` is a dict with

    * ``d_model``   -- int, the frozen backbone's hidden size.
    * ``vocab``     -- int, the vocabulary the block is scored over.
    * ``block_len`` -- int, ``L``: how many positions the block covers.
    * ``top_k``     -- int, ``K``: how many candidates per position you return.
    * ``cost_c``    -- float, the per-submitted-position verification cost (see
                       "What is measured").  It may be 0.
    * ``device``    -- the torch device to build on.
    * ``lm_head_weight`` -- float32 ``(vocab, d_model)``, the frozen backbone's
                       own output embedding.  Initialising an output projection
                       from it is what Medusa does and is usually much better
                       than random.
    * ``shared_proj`` -- an ``nn.Linear(d_model, vocab, bias=False)`` already
                       initialised from ``lm_head_weight``.  Referencing this
                       one module from every block position costs its parameters
                       **once**; building your own projection per position costs
                       them once per position.  That is a real budget decision,
                       not a formality -- see "Parameter budget".  It is rebuilt
                       identically in both processes, so if you keep it FROZEN
                       you can hold it outside the returned module (e.g. in a
                       list attribute) and keep it out of the checkpoint.

``loss(module, hidden, tokens, aux) -> torch.Tensor``

    THE TRAINING OBJECTIVE -- return a scalar to be back-propagated.  The fixed
    driver calls it several times per optimiser step, on consecutive
    micro-batches, and accumulates the gradients; ``aux["n_micro"]`` says how
    many.  That is a memory decision on the harness's part and changes nothing
    about the objective: write ``loss`` as if it saw one batch.

    * ``hidden`` -- float32 ``(B, S, d_model)``, the FROZEN backbone's hidden
      state after each of ``S`` consecutive tokens.  Detached: no gradient flows
      into the backbone, which never trains.
    * ``tokens`` -- int64 ``(B, S + L)``.  ``tokens[b, t + k]`` is the token
      ``k`` positions after the one ``hidden[b, t]`` was produced by, so
      ``tokens[:, k : k + S]`` is the target sequence for block position ``k``.
    * ``aux``    -- dict with ``step``, ``total_steps``, ``n_micro`` and
      ``generator`` (a seeded ``torch.Generator``).  Draw any randomness your
      objective needs -- a diffusion noise level, a masking pattern -- from that
      generator, so the run stays a function of the seed.  It also carries the
      **target model's own opinion**, cached once by the harness:

        - ``aux["target_top"]``  -- int64 ``(B, S + L - 1, KD)``
        - ``aux["target_logp"]`` -- float32 ``(B, S + L - 1, KD)``

      ``target_top[b, p]`` are the target's ``KD`` most likely tokens for stream
      position ``p + 1``, with their log-probabilities, teacher-forced on the
      stream.  The training stream is made of the TARGET's own greedy answers to
      a set of training prompts (chat, code and math requests), so ``tokens``
      after a position are the target's greedy continuation of it.  For block position ``k`` (1-based) at hidden index ``t`` the
      relevant entry is ``[:, t + k - 1]``; the slice for a whole window is
      ``[:, k - 1 : k - 1 + S]``.

      Distilling from the full distribution rather than the argmax ``tokens``
      is what the EAGLE family of drafters does; training on ``tokens`` is what
      Medusa does.  Both are legitimate.

``propose(module, hidden) -> (cand_token, cand_logp, n_submit)``

    The block, from ONE backbone forward.  ``hidden`` is float32 ``(B,
    d_model)``: one vector per item, the backbone's hidden state at the position
    a decoding round starts from.  That is the entire input -- there are no
    tokens here, because at inference the continuation is exactly what is
    unknown.  It runs on the same device as training, in batches, and is called
    for every position a round could start from.

    Return
    * ``cand_token`` -- int ``(B, L, K)``, your ``K`` candidate vocabulary ids
      for each of the ``L`` block positions, **best first**.
    * ``cand_logp``  -- float ``(B, L, K)``, your log-probabilities for them.
      Recorded as a diagnostic; the metric does not read them.
    * ``n_submit``   -- int ``(B,)`` in ``[1, L]``, how many leading positions of
      the block you actually submit for verification.  Return ``L`` to submit
      the whole block.  Submitting fewer can only lower the accepted length, and
      pays off only when ``cfg["cost_c"] > 0``.

    No gradients, no model, no tokenizer, no target, no truth, and nothing about
    how you are scored.

Unlike the sibling `spec-*` tasks, whose child builds a fresh policy object per
item, **one object is built here and it persists across every evaluation item**,
because a trained head must.  Nothing is fed back between items -- no truth
enters this process and no score is returned -- so the most that persistence can
buy is transductive statistics over unlabelled features.

Parameter budget
----------------
Every trainable parameter of the module ``build`` returns is counted, and the
total is capped at 1.05x the largest baseline's.  Parameters shared between
block positions (``cfg["shared_proj"]``, or any module you reuse) are counted
once, because that is how ``nn.Module.parameters()`` counts them.  The cap is
generous -- Medusa's ``L - 1`` independent output projections set it -- so the
interesting designs are the ones that spend it on structure rather than on
copies of the vocabulary projection.

What is measured
----------------
``tau``, the tokens produced per decoding round -- the quantity Medusa, DFlash,
DFlash 2 and DSpark all report -- measured by decoding: the target's own greedy
answers to a set of held-out prompts are replayed round by round.  At a round
starting at position ``t`` let ``g_1, g_2, ...`` be the target's greedy
continuation.  The target verifies your submitted block in one forward and
accepts the longest prefix of ``g`` that your block's top-1 tokens match; that
same forward yields one more token for free, and the next round starts after it.

    tau     = (tokens produced) / (rounds),   k = the matching prefix within n_submit

and, where the setting prices verification,

    eff_tau = (tokens produced) / sum over rounds of (1 + cost_c * n_submit)

which is ``tau`` exactly when ``cost_c`` is 0.  Both are computed by a separate
process that holds the answers; this file never sees them.
"""
import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

# ----- BEGIN EDITABLE REGION -----
def _distill(logits, aux, k, S):

    `logits` is (B*S, V); the cached slice for block position k (1-based) at

    """

baselines.docstring:
DFlash: a block-diffusion objective over the whole block.

Reference: Jian Chen, Yesheng Liang, Zhijian Liu, "DFlash: Block Diffusion for
Flash Speculative Decoding", arXiv:2602.06036 (v1 2026-02-05, v2 2026-05-28),
accepted ICML 2026 (`icml.cc/virtual/2026/poster/64301`); code
`github.com/z-lab/dflash`.

Protocol ported: the block is produced by a **block-diffusion** (masked
denoising) head rather than by independent per-position predictions. Every
position attends to the current state of every other position, so the head is
trained to fill a partially-revealed block -- which is what gives a parallel
block intra-dependency without any position conditioning on a *choice* made
downstream. Training samples a mask ratio per batch and predicts the masked
positions; inference starts from a fully masked block and denoises it in a fixed
number of rounds, committing the most confident positions each round.

NAMED DEVIATION, AND IT IS THE LARGEST OF THE FOUR ARMS -- read this before
reading its score. In the released system the block-diffusion drafter is a
BACKBONE, and it is conditioned on the target model's hidden states injected
directly into the drafter's KV cache. This task fixes one frozen autoregressive
backbone so that arms differ only in the block head, so:

  * the diffusion runs over the head's own per-position features rather than
    over a diffusion backbone, and
  * there is NO target-hidden-state KV injection: the head sees only the frozen
    drafter's last hidden state.

What survives is the objective and the joint block structure; what does not is
the drafter architecture and the target conditioning, which are a large part of
what DFlash reports. **Consequently: if this arm lands at or below `medusa`,
that is evidence the deviation ate the method, NOT evidence against block
diffusion, and it is to be reported as NOT MEASURED rather than as defeated.**
This was pre-registered as the task's soft kill condition.

Test: `dflash` must beat `default` everywhere. Its denoising must be a real
iteration -- a run with `ROUNDS = 1` (one pass from the fully masked block) must
score strictly below the shipped `ROUNDS = 2`, otherwise the iteration is inert
and the arm is just a masked-position predictor.

The target-conditioning half of the method is partially restored relative to the
first draft of this port: the block the head denoises toward is the TARGET's own
teacher-forced top-1, and the per-position loss distils the target's top-k
distribution, rather than regressing on raw corpus tokens. What is still missing
is the target-hidden-state KV injection, which a frozen backbone cannot accept.

"""Parallel block head for speculative decoding (EDITABLE).

A speculative decoder proposes several tokens per target forward.  The cheapest
possible proposer runs the drafter ONCE and reads a whole block of ``L`` future
positions off that single forward -- but an ordinary autoregressive drafter has
nothing to say about position 2 from one forward, because position 2's
distribution is conditioned on position 1's token, which has not been chosen yet.
Measured on this harness's gpt2 pilot: the probability that the target's token
at position ``j`` is among the drafter's top-8 candidates was **0.96 at j = 1
and 0.01 at j = 2** -- the drafter is at chance from the second position on.

So a parallel block is not something a drafter *has*; it is something a block
head has to be *built and trained* to produce.  That is the question this file
answers, and the released systems answer it differently -- which is the whole
method:

* **Medusa** (arXiv:2401.10774): ``L - 1`` *independent* heads, one per offset,
  each predicting its position from ``h`` alone.  No intra-block dependency.
* **DFlash** (arXiv:2602.06036, ICML 2026): a *block diffusion* objective -- the
  whole block is denoised jointly, each position conditioned on the current
  state of all the others.
* **DFlash 2** (Inco AI, 2026): *local mixing* -- two-tap depthwise dynamic
  convolutions tie each position to its predecessor -- plus a learned pairwise
  **path selector** over the retained top-``K`` candidates.
* **DSpark** (arXiv:2607.05147): an explicit first-order **Markov transition
  bias** on the block logits, plus a **confidence head** predicting how far down
  the block the dependency still holds.

Everything else is fixed by the harness: the frozen drafter backbone, the
optimiser, the learning-rate schedule, the number of steps, the batch shape, the
token stream, the target model and the measurement.  **You design a module and
an objective; you do not design a training recipe.**

Interface contract
------------------
``build(cfg) -> torch.nn.Module``

    Construct and return the head.  Called ONCE, before training.  Everything
    the head needs at inference must live **inside the returned module** --
    parameters, or ``register_buffer`` for anything fitted but not trained --
    because training and proposing happen in two separate processes and only the
    module's ``state_dict`` travels between them.  ``cfg`` is a dict with

    * ``d_model``   -- int, the frozen backbone's hidden size.
    * ``vocab``     -- int, the vocabulary the block is scored over.
    * ``block_len`` -- int, ``L``: how many positions the block covers.
    * ``top_k``     -- int, ``K``: how many candidates per position you return.
    * ``cost_c``    -- float, the per-submitted-position verification cost (see
                       "What is measured").  It may be 0.
    * ``device``    -- the torch device to build on.
    * ``lm_head_weight`` -- float32 ``(vocab, d_model)``, the frozen backbone's
                       own output embedding.  Initialising an output projection
                       from it is what Medusa does and is usually much better
                       than random.
    * ``shared_proj`` -- an ``nn.Linear(d_model, vocab, bias=False)`` already
                       initialised from ``lm_head_weight``.  Referencing this
                       one module from every block position costs its parameters
                       **once**; building your own projection per position costs
                       them once per position.  That is a real budget decision,
                       not a formality -- see "Parameter budget".  It is rebuilt
                       identically in both processes, so if you keep it FROZEN
                       you can hold it outside the returned module (e.g. in a
                       list attribute) and keep it out of the checkpoint.

``loss(module, hidden, tokens, aux) -> torch.Tensor``

    THE TRAINING OBJECTIVE -- return a scalar to be back-propagated.  The fixed
    driver calls it several times per optimiser step, on consecutive
    micro-batches, and accumulates the gradients; ``aux["n_micro"]`` says how
    many.  That is a memory decision on the harness's part and changes nothing
    about the objective: write ``loss`` as if it saw one batch.

    * ``hidden`` -- float32 ``(B, S, d_model)``, the FROZEN backbone's hidden
      state after each of ``S`` consecutive tokens.  Detached: no gradient flows
      into the backbone, which never trains.
    * ``tokens`` -- int64 ``(B, S + L)``.  ``tokens[b, t + k]`` is the token
      ``k`` positions after the one ``hidden[b, t]`` was produced by, so
      ``tokens[:, k : k + S]`` is the target sequence for block position ``k``.
    * ``aux``    -- dict with ``step``, ``total_steps``, ``n_micro`` and
      ``generator`` (a seeded ``torch.Generator``).  Draw any randomness your
      objective needs -- a diffusion noise level, a masking pattern -- from that
      generator, so the run stays a function of the seed.  It also carries the
      **target model's own opinion**, cached once by the harness:

        - ``aux["target_top"]``  -- int64 ``(B, S + L - 1, KD)``
        - ``aux["target_logp"]`` -- float32 ``(B, S + L - 1, KD)``

      ``target_top[b, p]`` are the target's ``KD`` most likely tokens for stream
      position ``p + 1``, with their log-probabilities, teacher-forced on the
      stream.  The training stream is made of the TARGET's own greedy answers to
      a set of training prompts (chat, code and math requests), so ``tokens``
      after a position are the target's greedy continuation of it.  For block position ``k`` (1-based) at hidden index ``t`` the
      relevant entry is ``[:, t + k - 1]``; the slice for a whole window is
      ``[:, k - 1 : k - 1 + S]``.

      Distilling from the full distribution rather than the argmax ``tokens``
      is what the EAGLE family of drafters does; training on ``tokens`` is what
      Medusa does.  Both are legitimate.

``propose(module, hidden) -> (cand_token, cand_logp, n_submit)``

    The block, from ONE backbone forward.  ``hidden`` is float32 ``(B,
    d_model)``: one vector per item, the backbone's hidden state at the position
    a decoding round starts from.  That is the entire input -- there are no
    tokens here, because at inference the continuation is exactly what is
    unknown.  It runs on the same device as training, in batches, and is called
    for every position a round could start from.

    Return
    * ``cand_token`` -- int ``(B, L, K)``, your ``K`` candidate vocabulary ids
      for each of the ``L`` block positions, **best first**.
    * ``cand_logp``  -- float ``(B, L, K)``, your log-probabilities for them.
      Recorded as a diagnostic; the metric does not read them.
    * ``n_submit``   -- int ``(B,)`` in ``[1, L]``, how many leading positions of
      the block you actually submit for verification.  Return ``L`` to submit
      the whole block.  Submitting fewer can only lower the accepted length, and
      pays off only when ``cfg["cost_c"] > 0``.

    No gradients, no model, no tokenizer, no target, no truth, and nothing about
    how you are scored.

Unlike the sibling `spec-*` tasks, whose child builds a fresh policy object per
item, **one object is built here and it persists across every evaluation item**,
because a trained head must.  Nothing is fed back between items -- no truth
enters this process and no score is returned -- so the most that persistence can
buy is transductive statistics over unlabelled features.

Parameter budget
----------------
Every trainable parameter of the module ``build`` returns is counted, and the
total is capped at 1.05x the largest baseline's.  Parameters shared between
block positions (``cfg["shared_proj"]``, or any module you reuse) are counted
once, because that is how ``nn.Module.parameters()`` counts them.  The cap is
generous -- Medusa's ``L - 1`` independent output projections set it -- so the
interesting designs are the ones that spend it on structure rather than on
copies of the vocabulary projection.

What is measured
----------------
``tau``, the tokens produced per decoding round -- the quantity Medusa, DFlash,
DFlash 2 and DSpark all report -- measured by decoding: the target's own greedy
answers to a set of held-out prompts are replayed round by round.  At a round
starting at position ``t`` let ``g_1, g_2, ...`` be the target's greedy
continuation.  The target verifies your submitted block in one forward and
accepts the longest prefix of ``g`` that your block's top-1 tokens match; that
same forward yields one more token for free, and the next round starts after it.

    tau     = (tokens produced) / (rounds),   k = the matching prefix within n_submit

and, where the setting prices verification,

    eff_tau = (tokens produced) / sum over rounds of (1 + cost_c * n_submit)

which is ``tau`` exactly when ``cost_c`` is 0.  Both are computed by a separate
process that holds the answers; this file never sees them.

        self.inp = nn.Linear(d_state, d)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.inp.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.inp.bias)

        k = k.view(N, L, self.n_head, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)
        v = v.view(N, L, self.n_head, self.dh).transpose(1, 2)
        a = torch.softmax((q @ k.transpose(-2, -1)) / (self.dh ** 0.5), dim=-1)
        return self.out((a @ v).transpose(1, 2).reshape(N, L, d))

    def forward(self, h, state):
        """h (N, d); state (N, L) int64 with `vocab` marking a masked slot."""
        x = h[:, None, :] + self.pos[None, :, :] + self.inp(self.tok(state))

    """DFlash (arXiv:2602.06036, ICML 2026): block diffusion over the block."""

    D_STATE = 64
    N_HEAD = 8
    ROUNDS = 2

    def build(self, cfg):
        self.cfg = cfg
        proj = cfg["shared_proj"].to(cfg["device"])
        m = _BlockDiffusion(cfg["d_model"], cfg["vocab"], cfg["block_len"],
                            self.D_STATE, self.N_HEAD, proj)

        del tokens
        L, V = self.cfg["block_len"], self.cfg["vocab"]
        S = hidden.shape[1]
        h = hidden.reshape(-1, hidden.shape[-1])
        # the block the head is denoising toward is the TARGET's own top-1 at
        # each position, which is what the metric rewards agreement with

        # the objective stays a function of the seed
        u = torch.rand((), generator=aux["generator"]).item() * 0.9 + 0.1

        state = torch.where(keep, blk, torch.full_like(blk, V))

        masked = ~keep
        if not bool(masked.any()):
            masked = torch.ones_like(keep)
        # distil each position toward the target's distribution, weighted by how
        # often that position was actually masked in this draw -- an unmasked
        # slot was handed its answer and teaches the head nothing
        total = hidden.new_zeros(())
        for k in range(L):
            w = float(masked[:, k].float().mean())
            if w > 0.0:

    def propose(self, module, hidden):
        L, K, V = self.cfg["block_len"], self.cfg["top_k"], self.cfg["vocab"]
        B = hidden.shape[0]
        state = torch.full((B, L), V, dtype=torch.long, device=hidden.device)
        lg = None
        per = max(1, (L + self.ROUNDS - 1) // self.ROUNDS)
        for r in range(self.ROUNDS):
            lg = module(hidden, state).float()
            if r == self.ROUNDS - 1:

            lp = torch.log_softmax(lg, dim=-1)
            conf, arg = lp.max(dim=-1)
            conf = conf.masked_fill(state != V, -1e30)
            take = torch.topk(conf, min(per, L), dim=1).indices
            state = state.scatter(1, take, arg.gather(1, take))
        lp = torch.log_softmax(lg, dim=-1)
        v, i = torch.topk(lp, K, dim=-1)

        # first token, conditioned only on h -- so it is the frozen backbone's own
        # next-token distribution (as `default`/`medusa` emit), not the diffusion

        # degrades position 1 below the frozen lm_head under the fixed step budget

        # diffusion, which is the objective over positions 2..L).
        lp0 = torch.log_softmax(hidden.float() @ self.cfg["lm_head_weight"].float().t(), -1)
        v0, i0 = torch.topk(lp0, K, dim=-1)
        i = i.clone(); v = v.clone()
        i[:, 0] = i0
        v[:, 0] = v0
        n_submit = np.full(B, L, dtype=np.int64)
        return i, v, n_submit

Reference: Inco AI, "DFlash 2: Keep Drafting Parallel", blog post, August 2026,
`https://inco.ai/blog/dflash2/`.  Checkpoints `incoai/Qwen3.8-27B-DFlash2` and
`incoai/Muse-Glimmer-30B-DFlash2`.

PROVENANCE CAVEAT, recorded rather than smoothed over: **DFlash 2 is NOT a
paper.** There is no arXiv id and no peer review. It is a vendor blog post with
released checkpoints. It is nonetheless a *checkable* reference, which is what
this repo's baseline-provenance rule asks for, and the DFlash repo's own README
cites it that way:

    @misc{inco2026dflash2,
      title  = {DFlash 2: Keep Drafting Parallel},
      author = {{Inco AI}},
      year   = {2026}, month = {August},
      url    = {https://inco.ai/blog/dflash2/}}

Protocol ported, as the post states it:
  * **two-tap depthwise dynamic convolutions** mix each block position with its
    predecessor to fight suffix decay. The two tap weights are generated per
    channel from the position's own feature (that is what makes them *dynamic*)
    and normalised over the two taps.
  * **top-k retention plus a path selector**: rather than committing to the
    per-position argmax, keep `K` candidates per position and score ADJACENT
    CANDIDATE PAIRS with a low-rank bilinear form, then trace the single
    best-scoring path (Viterbi) through the retained lattice. The post's
    motivation is the gap between top-1 being right and the truth merely being
    retained -- 85.4% against 99.5% at their scale.

Named deviations:
  * **the convolutions move from the backbone to the head.** In the released
    system the two-tap dynamic convolutions sit INSIDE the drafter backbone,
    around attention and FFN. This task holds one frozen backbone fixed so that
    arms differ only in the block head, so they are ported as convolutions over
    the head's own per-position features. This is the deviation the predecessor
    task declared "out of scope by construction"; here it is the arm.
  * **scale.** The released checkpoints are 27B and 30B and are never loaded;
    the mechanism is ported at the gpt2 / Qwen-0.5B scale this family bakes, with
    `K = 8` retained candidates rather than the post's 16 because `K` is a
    harness constant shared by every arm.
  * one SHARED output projection across positions, so the arm's budget goes to
    the convolutions and the selector rather than to copies of the vocabulary
    projection.

Test: `dflash2` must beat `default` everywhere; and because the selector can
only reorder candidates the head already retained, its `topk_*` diagnostics must
match a run with the selector disabled while its `top1_*` differ -- that is the
selector doing its job rather than the convolutions alone.

_FILE = "speculative-sampling/mlsb_blockhead.py"

_CONTENT = '''\
def _distill(logits, aux, k, S):
    """Soft cross-entropy against the TARGET's cached top-KD at block position k.

    `logits` is (B*S, V); the cached slice for block position k (1-based) at
    hidden index t is aux["target_top"][:, t + k - 1], so the whole window is
    [:, k-1 : k-1+S].  The target's log-probs are renormalised over its own
    top-KD support, which is the usual truncated-distillation objective.
    """
    top = aux["target_top"][:, k - 1:k - 1 + S]
    ids = top.reshape(-1, top.shape[-1])
    w = torch.softmax(aux["target_logp"][:, k - 1:k - 1 + S].reshape(ids.shape), -1)
    return -(w * torch.log_softmax(logits, -1).gather(-1, ids)).sum(-1).mean()


class _ResBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(d, d)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.linear.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.linear.bias)
        self.act = nn.SiLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.act(self.linear(x))


class _DFlash2(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, vocab, L, rank, proj):
        super().__init__()
        self.L, self.rank = L, rank
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(L, d))
        self.block = _ResBlock(d)
        # two-tap DEPTHWISE DYNAMIC convolution: per channel, per position, the
        # tap weights are produced from that position's own feature
        self.dyn = nn.Linear(d, 2 * d)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.dyn.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.dyn.bias)
        self.post = _ResBlock(d)
        self.proj = proj                        # SHARED across all L positions
        # low-rank bilinear pairwise path selector
        self.emb = nn.Embedding(vocab, rank)
        nn.init.normal_(self.emb.weight, std=0.02)
        self.M = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(rank, rank))
        nn.init.normal_(self.M, std=0.02)
        self.alpha = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(()))

    def feats(self, h):
        f = self.block(h[:, None, :] + self.pos[None, :, :])        # (B, L, d)
        d = f.shape[-1]
        taps = self.dyn(f).view(f.shape[0], self.L, d, 2)
        taps = torch.softmax(taps, dim=-1)
        prev = torch.cat([f[:, :1], f[:, :-1]], dim=1)              # f_{k-1}
        f = taps[..., 0] * f + taps[..., 1] * prev
        return self.post(f)

    def pair(self, prev_ids, cand_ids):
        """Low-rank bilinear score between a previous token and candidates."""
        a = self.emb(prev_ids)                                      # (..., r)
        b = self.emb(cand_ids)                                      # (..., K, r)
        return torch.einsum("...r,rs,...ks->...k", a, self.M, b)


class CustomBlockHead:
    """DFlash 2 (Inco AI, 2026): dynamic two-tap mixing + pairwise path search."""

    RANK = 32

    def build(self, cfg):
        self.cfg = cfg
        proj = cfg["shared_proj"].to(cfg["device"])
        m = _DFlash2(cfg["d_model"], cfg["vocab"], cfg["block_len"], self.RANK, proj)
        return m.to(cfg["device"])

    def loss(self, module, hidden, tokens, aux):
        L, K, V = self.cfg["block_len"], self.cfg["top_k"], self.cfg["vocab"]
        S = hidden.shape[1]
        f = module.feats(hidden.reshape(-1, hidden.shape[-1]))
        total = hidden.new_zeros(())
        for k in range(L):
            lg = module.proj(f[:, k])
            tgt = aux["target_top"][:, k:k + S, 0].reshape(-1)   # the target's own top-1
            total = total + _distill(lg, aux, k + 1, S)
            if k > 0:
                # train the selector to pick the true token out of the retained
                # candidates, given the true previous token
                with torch.no_grad():
                    cand = torch.topk(lg, K, dim=-1).indices
                hit = (cand == tgt[:, None])
                keep = hit.any(-1)
                if bool(keep.any()):
                    prev = tokens[:, k:k + S].reshape(-1)[keep]
                    c = cand[keep]
                    sc = module.alpha * module.pair(prev, c) \\
                        + torch.gather(torch.log_softmax(lg[keep], -1), 1, c)
                    total = total + nn.functional.cross_entropy(
                        sc, hit[keep].float().argmax(-1))
        return total

    def propose(self, module, hidden):
        L, K = self.cfg["block_len"], self.cfg["top_k"]
        B = hidden.shape[0]
        f = module.feats(hidden)
        lp, ids = [], []
        for k in range(L):
            v, i = torch.topk(torch.log_softmax(module.proj(f[:, k]).float(), -1),
                              K, dim=-1)
            lp.append(v)
            ids.append(i)
        lp = torch.stack(lp, 1)                                   # (B, L, K)
        ids = torch.stack(ids, 1)
        # Position 1 has no predecessor to mix with (the dynamic conv) or to select
        # against (the path search), so it is the frozen backbone's own next-token
        # distribution -- what `default`/`medusa` emit at position 1 -- rather than
        # the trained shared projection, whose position-0 output the fixed step
        # budget degrades below the lm_head at the larger vocabulary. The two-tap
        # convolutions and the pairwise selector -- the method -- still shape
        # positions 2..L through the transition scores.
        lp0 = torch.log_softmax(hidden.float() @ self.cfg["lm_head_weight"].float().t(), -1)
        v0, i0 = torch.topk(lp0, K, dim=-1)
        ids = ids.clone(); lp = lp.clone()
        ids[:, 0] = i0
        lp[:, 0] = v0
        # Viterbi over the retained lattice: emission = the head's own log-prob,
        # transition = the bilinear pair score between adjacent candidates
        score = lp[:, 0].clone()
        back = torch.zeros(B, L, K, dtype=torch.long, device=hidden.device)
        for k in range(1, L):
            trans = module.alpha * torch.einsum(
                "bpr,rs,bqs->bpq", module.emb(ids[:, k - 1]), module.M,
                module.emb(ids[:, k])).float()
            tot = score[:, :, None] + trans + lp[:, k][:, None, :]
            score, back[:, k] = tot.max(dim=1)
        path = torch.zeros(B, L, dtype=torch.long, device=hidden.device)
        cur = score.argmax(dim=1)
        for k in range(L - 1, -1, -1):
            path[:, k] = cur
            cur = back[:, k].gather(1, cur[:, None]).squeeze(1)
        # put the chosen candidate first: the metric reads index 0, and the
        # selector's whole job is to decide which retained candidate that is
        order = torch.argsort((torch.arange(K, device=hidden.device)[None, None, :]
                               == path[:, :, None]).long(), dim=-1, descending=True,
                              stable=True)
        ids = torch.gather(ids, 2, order)
        lp = torch.gather(lp, 2, order)
        n_submit = np.full(B, L, dtype=np.int64)
        return ids, lp, n_submit

"""Parallel block head for speculative decoding (EDITABLE).

A speculative decoder proposes several tokens per target forward.  The cheapest
possible proposer runs the drafter ONCE and reads a whole block of ``L`` future
positions off that single forward -- but an ordinary autoregressive drafter has
nothing to say about position 2 from one forward, because position 2's
distribution is conditioned on position 1's token, which has not been chosen yet.
Measured on this harness's gpt2 pilot: the probability that the target's token
at position ``j`` is among the drafter's top-8 candidates was **0.96 at j = 1
and 0.01 at j = 2** -- the drafter is at chance from the second position on.

So a parallel block is not something a drafter *has*; it is something a block
head has to be *built and trained* to produce.  That is the question this file
answers, and the released systems answer it differently -- which is the whole
method:

* **Medusa** (arXiv:2401.10774): ``L - 1`` *independent* heads, one per offset,
  each predicting its position from ``h`` alone.  No intra-block dependency.
* **DFlash** (arXiv:2602.06036, ICML 2026): a *block diffusion* objective -- the
  whole block is denoised jointly, each position conditioned on the current
  state of all the others.
* **DFlash 2** (Inco AI, 2026): *local mixing* -- two-tap depthwise dynamic
  convolutions tie each position to its predecessor -- plus a learned pairwise
  **path selector** over the retained top-``K`` candidates.
* **DSpark** (arXiv:2607.05147): an explicit first-order **Markov transition
  bias** on the block logits, plus a **confidence head** predicting how far down
  the block the dependency still holds.

Everything else is fixed by the harness: the frozen drafter backbone, the
optimiser, the learning-rate schedule, the number of steps, the batch shape, the
token stream, the target model and the measurement.  **You design a module and
an objective; you do not design a training recipe.**

Interface contract
------------------
``build(cfg) -> torch.nn.Module``

    Construct and return the head.  Called ONCE, before training.  Everything
    the head needs at inference must live **inside the returned module** --
    parameters, or ``register_buffer`` for anything fitted but not trained --
    because training and proposing happen in two separate processes and only the
    module's ``state_dict`` travels between them.  ``cfg`` is a dict with

    * ``d_model``   -- int, the frozen backbone's hidden size.
    * ``vocab``     -- int, the vocabulary the block is scored over.
    * ``block_len`` -- int, ``L``: how many positions the block covers.
    * ``top_k``     -- int, ``K``: how many candidates per position you return.
    * ``cost_c``    -- float, the per-submitted-position verification cost (see
                       "What is measured").  It may be 0.
    * ``device``    -- the torch device to build on.
    * ``lm_head_weight`` -- float32 ``(vocab, d_model)``, the frozen backbone's
                       own output embedding.  Initialising an output projection
                       from it is what Medusa does and is usually much better
                       than random.
    * ``shared_proj`` -- an ``nn.Linear(d_model, vocab, bias=False)`` already
                       initialised from ``lm_head_weight``.  Referencing this
                       one module from every block position costs its parameters
                       **once**; building your own projection per position costs
                       them once per position.  That is a real budget decision,
                       not a formality -- see "Parameter budget".  It is rebuilt
                       identically in both processes, so if you keep it FROZEN
                       you can hold it outside the returned module (e.g. in a
                       list attribute) and keep it out of the checkpoint.

``loss(module, hidden, tokens, aux) -> torch.Tensor``

    THE TRAINING OBJECTIVE -- return a scalar to be back-propagated.  The fixed
    driver calls it several times per optimiser step, on consecutive
    micro-batches, and accumulates the gradients; ``aux["n_micro"]`` says how
    many.  That is a memory decision on the harness's part and changes nothing
    about the objective: write ``loss`` as if it saw one batch.

    * ``hidden`` -- float32 ``(B, S, d_model)``, the FROZEN backbone's hidden
      state after each of ``S`` consecutive tokens.  Detached: no gradient flows
      into the backbone, which never trains.
    * ``tokens`` -- int64 ``(B, S + L)``.  ``tokens[b, t + k]`` is the token
      ``k`` positions after the one ``hidden[b, t]`` was produced by, so
      ``tokens[:, k : k + S]`` is the target sequence for block position ``k``.
    * ``aux``    -- dict with ``step``, ``total_steps``, ``n_micro`` and
      ``generator`` (a seeded ``torch.Generator``).  Draw any randomness your
      objective needs -- a diffusion noise level, a masking pattern -- from that
      generator, so the run stays a function of the seed.  It also carries the
      **target model's own opinion**, cached once by the harness:

        - ``aux["target_logp"]`` -- float32 ``(B, S + L - 1, KD)``

      ``target_top[b, p]`` are the target's ``KD`` most likely tokens for stream
      position ``p + 1``, with their log-probabilities, teacher-forced on the

      a set of training prompts (chat, code and math requests), so ``tokens``
      after a position are the target's greedy continuation of it.  For block position ``k`` (1-based) at hidden index ``t`` the

      Medusa does.  Both are legitimate.

    The block, from ONE backbone forward.  ``hidden`` is float32 ``(B,
    d_model)``: one vector per item, the backbone's hidden state at the position
    a decoding round starts from.  That is the entire input -- there are no
    tokens here, because at inference the continuation is exactly what is
    unknown.  It runs on the same device as training, in batches, and is called
    for every position a round could start from.

    Return

      for each of the ``L`` block positions, **best first**.
    * ``cand_logp``  -- float ``(B, L, K)``, your log-probabilities for them.
      Recorded as a diagnostic; the metric does not read them.
    * ``n_submit``   -- int ``(B,)`` in ``[1, L]``, how many leading positions of
      the block you actually submit for verification.  Return ``L`` to submit
      the whole block.  Submitting fewer can only lower the accepted length, and
      pays off only when ``cfg["cost_c"] > 0``.

    how you are scored.

Unlike the sibling `spec-*` tasks, whose child builds a fresh policy object per
item, **one object is built here and it persists across every evaluation item**,
because a trained head must.  Nothing is fed back between items -- no truth
enters this process and no score is returned -- so the most that persistence can
buy is transductive statistics over unlabelled features.

----------------
Every trainable parameter of the module ``build`` returns is counted, and the
total is capped at 1.05x the largest baseline's.  Parameters shared between

once, because that is how ``nn.Module.parameters()`` counts them.  The cap is
generous -- Medusa's ``L - 1`` independent output projections set it -- so the
interesting designs are the ones that spend it on structure rather than on
copies of the vocabulary projection.

----------------
``tau``, the tokens produced per decoding round -- the quantity Medusa, DFlash,
DFlash 2 and DSpark all report -- measured by decoding: the target's own greedy
answers to a set of held-out prompts are replayed round by round.  At a round
starting at position ``t`` let ``g_1, g_2, ...`` be the target's greedy
continuation.  The target verifies your submitted block in one forward and
accepts the longest prefix of ``g`` that your block's top-1 tokens match; that
same forward yields one more token for free, and the next round starts after it.

    tau     = (tokens produced) / (rounds),   k = the matching prefix within n_submit

and, where the setting prices verification,

    eff_tau = (tokens produced) / sum over rounds of (1 + cost_c * n_submit)

import numpy as np
import torch
import torch.nn as nn

def _distill(logits, aux, k, S):
    """Soft cross-entropy against the TARGET's cached top-KD at block position k.

    `logits` is (B*S, V); the cached slice for block position k (1-based) at
    hidden index t is aux["target_top"][:, t + k - 1], so the whole window is
    [:, k-1 : k-1+S].  The target's log-probs are renormalised over its own
    top-KD support, which is the usual truncated-distillation objective.
    """
    top = aux["target_top"][:, k - 1:k - 1 + S]
    ids = top.reshape(-1, top.shape[-1])
    w = torch.softmax(aux["target_logp"][:, k - 1:k - 1 + S].reshape(ids.shape), -1)
    return -(w * torch.log_softmax(logits, -1).gather(-1, ids)).sum(-1).mean()


class _ResBlock(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d):
        super().__init__()
        self.linear = nn.Linear(d, d)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.linear.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.linear.bias)
        self.act = nn.SiLU()

    def forward(self, x):
        return x + self.act(self.linear(x))


class _DFlash2(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self, d, vocab, L, rank, proj):
        super().__init__()
        self.L, self.rank = L, rank
        self.pos = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(L, d))
        self.block = _ResBlock(d)
        # two-tap DEPTHWISE DYNAMIC convolution: per channel, per position, the
        # tap weights are produced from that position's own feature
        self.dyn = nn.Linear(d, 2 * d)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.dyn.weight)
        nn.init.zeros_(self.dyn.bias)
        self.post = _ResBlock(d)
        self.proj = proj                        # SHARED across all L positions
        # low-rank bilinear pairwise path selector
        self.emb = nn.Embedding(vocab, rank)
        nn.init.normal_(self.emb.weight, std=0.02)
        self.M = nn.Parameter(torch.zeros(rank, rank))
        nn.init.normal_(self.M, std=0.02)
        self.alpha = nn.Parameter(torch.ones(()))

    def feats(self, h):
        f = self.block(h[:, None, :] + self.pos[None, :, :])        # (B, L, d)
        d = f.shape[-1]
        taps = self.dyn(f).view(f.shape[0], self.L, d, 2)
        taps = torch.softmax(taps, dim=-1)
        prev = torch.cat([f[:, :1], f[:, :-1]], dim=1)              # f_{k-1}
        f = taps[..., 0] * f + taps[..., 1] * prev
        return self.post(f)

    def pair(self, prev_ids, cand_ids):
        """Low-rank bilinear score between a previous token and candidates."""
        a = self.emb(prev_ids)                                      # (..., r)
        b = self.emb(cand_ids)                                      # (..., K, r)
        return torch.einsum("...r,rs,...ks->...k", a, self.M, b)

    """DFlash 2 (Inco AI, 2026): dynamic two-tap mixing + pairwise path search."""

    RANK = 32

    def build(self, cfg):
        self.cfg = cfg
        proj = cfg["shared_proj"].to(cfg["device"])
        m = _DFlash2(cfg["d_model"], cfg["vocab"], cfg["block_len"], self.RANK, proj)
        return m.to(cfg["device"])

    def loss(self, module, hidden, tokens, aux):
        L, K, V = self.cfg["block_len"], self.cfg["top_k"], self.cfg["vocab"]
        S = hidden.shape[1]
        f = module.feats(hidden.reshape(-1, hidden.shape[-1]))
        total = hidden.new_zeros(())
        for k in range(L):
            lg = module.proj(f[:, k])
            tgt = aux["target_top"][:, k:k + S, 0].reshape(-1)   # the target's own top-1
            total = total + _distill(lg, aux, k + 1, S)
            if k > 0:
                # train the selector to pick the true token out of the retained
                # candidates, given the true previous token
                with torch.no_grad():
                    cand = torch.topk(lg, K, dim=-1).indices
                hit = (cand == tgt[:, None])
                keep = hit.any(-1)
                if bool(keep.any()):
                    prev = tokens[:, k:k + S].reshape(-1)[keep]
                    c = cand[keep]
                    sc = module.alpha * module.pair(prev, c) \
                        + torch.gather(torch.log_softmax(lg[keep], -1), 1, c)
                    total = total + nn.functional.cross_entropy(
                        sc, hit[keep].float().argmax(-1))
        return total

        L, K = self.cfg["block_len"], self.cfg["top_k"]
        B = hidden.shape[0]
        f = module.feats(hidden)
        lp, ids = [], []
        for k in range(L):
            v, i = torch.topk(torch.log_softmax(module.proj(f[:, k]).float(), -1),
                              K, dim=-1)
            lp.append(v)
            ids.append(i)
        lp = torch.stack(lp, 1)                                   # (B, L, K)
        ids = torch.stack(ids, 1)
        # Position 1 has no predecessor to mix with (the dynamic conv) or to select
        # against (the path search), so it is the frozen backbone's own next-token
        # distribution -- what `default`/`medusa` emit at position 1 -- rather than
        # the trained shared projection, whose position-0 output the fixed step
        # budget degrades below the lm_head at the larger vocabulary. The two-tap
        # convolutions and the pairwise selector -- the method -- still shape
        # positions 2..L through the transition scores.
        lp0 = torch.log_softmax(hidden.float() @ self.cfg["lm_head_weight"].float().t(), -1)
        v0, i0 = torch.topk(lp0, K, dim=-1)
        ids = ids.clone(); lp = lp.clone()
        ids[:, 0] = i0
        lp[:, 0] = v0

        # transition = the bilinear pair score between adjacent candidates
        score = lp[:, 0].clone()

            trans = module.alpha * torch.einsum(
                "bpr,rs,bqs->bpq", module.emb(ids[:, k - 1]), module.M,
                module.emb(ids[:, k])).float()

            score, back[:, k] = tot.max(dim=1)

            cur = back[:, k].gather(1, cur[:, None]).squeeze(1)

        # selector's whole job is to decide which retained candidate that is

                               == path[:, :, None]).long(), dim=-1, descending=True,
                              stable=True)

        lp = torch.gather(lp, 2, order)

        return ids, lp, n_submit

Huishuai Zhang, Dongyan Zhao, Wenfeng Liang (DeepSeek-AI + Peking University),
"DSpark: Confidence-Scheduled Speculative Decoding with Semi-Autoregressive
Generation", arXiv:2607.05147; code `github.com/deepseek-ai/DeepSpec` (MIT).

  * a **sequential Markov head** injects first-order dependency as a LOW-RANK
    transition bias on the draft logits, `B(x_{k-1}, .) = W1[x_{k-1}] W2` with
    `W1 in R^{V x r}` and `W2 in R^{r x V}`, applied position by position to the
    token actually chosen at `k-1`;
  * a **confidence head** `c_k = sigma(w^T [h_k ; W1[x_{k-1}]])` predicts the
    per-position conditional acceptance probability;
  * verification length is **scheduled** from the cumulative survival
    `a_j = prod_{i<=j} c_i`: positions are admitted in order while the predicted
    throughput `Theta(B) = (1 + sum_{j<=B} a_j) / (1 + c * B)` is still rising.
    At `cost_c = 0` that objective is monotone in B, so the whole block is
    submitted -- which is the correct behaviour, not a special case: DSpark's own
    rule admits while throughput increases, and with free verification it always
    does.

    build had to shrink it to 32 to fit the shared budget; at the Qwen2.5
    7B / 0.5B-1.5B pairs the paper's rank fits well inside Medusa's cap.)

    hidden state. This task fixes one frozen autoregressive backbone, which
    emits a single `h`, so the per-position features the Markov and confidence
    heads consume are produced by this head itself from `h` and a positional
    code. This is the unavoidable consequence of holding the backbone fixed so
    that arms differ only in the block head.

    parallel backbone's own head. This is what makes DSpark the parameter-cheap
    arm, which is faithful: its dependency lives in a low-rank bias, not in
    copies of the vocabulary projection.

admit until throughput starts *declining*; a flat stretch is not a decline.

"""Parallel block head for speculative decoding (EDITABLE).

A speculative decoder proposes several tokens per target forward.  The cheapest
possible proposer runs the drafter ONCE and reads a whole block of ``L`` future
positions off that single forward -- but an ordinary autoregressive drafter has
nothing to say about position 2 from one forward, because position 2's
distribution is conditioned on position 1's token, which has not been chosen yet.
Measured on this harness's gpt2 pilot: the probability that the target's token
at position ``j`` is among the drafter's top-8 candidates was **0.96 at j = 1
and 0.01 at j = 2** -- the drafter is at chance from the second position on.

So a parallel block is not something a drafter *has*; it is something a block
head has to be *built and trained* to produce.  That is the question this file
answers, and the released systems answer it differently -- which is the whole
method:

* **Medusa** (arXiv:2401.10774): ``L - 1`` *independent* heads, one per offset,
  each predicting its position from ``h`` alone.  No intra-block dependency.
* **DFlash** (arXiv:2602.06036, ICML 2026): a *block diffusion* objective -- the
  whole block is denoised jointly, each position conditioned on the current
  state of all the others.
* **DFlash 2** (Inco AI, 2026): *local mixing* -- two-tap depthwise dynamic
  convolutions tie each position to its predecessor -- plus a learned pairwise
  **path selector** over the retained top-``K`` candidates.
* **DSpark** (arXiv:2607.05147): an explicit first-order **Markov transition
  bias** on the block logits, plus a **confidence head** predicting how far down
  the block the dependency still holds.

Everything else is fixed by the harness: the frozen drafter backbone, the
optimiser, the learning-rate schedule, the number of steps, the batch shape, the
token stream, the target model and the measurement.  **You design a module and
an objective; you do not design a training recipe.**

Interface contract
------------------
``build(cfg) -> torch.nn.Module``

    Construct and return the head.  Called ONCE, before training.  Everything
    the head needs at inference must live **inside the returned module** --
    parameters, or ``register_buffer`` for anything fitted but not trained --
    because training and proposing happen in two separate processes and only the
    module's ``state_dict`` travels between them.  ``cfg`` is a dict with

    * ``d_model``   -- int, the frozen backbone's hidden size.
    * ``vocab``     -- int, the vocabulary the block is scored over.
    * ``block_len`` -- int, ``L``: how many positions the block covers.
    * ``top_k``     -- int, ``K``: how many candidates per position you return.
    * ``cost_c``    -- float, the per-submitted-position verification cost (see
                       "What is measured").  It may be 0.
    * ``device``    -- the torch device to build on.
    * ``lm_head_weight`` -- float32 ``(vocab, d_model)``, the frozen backbone's
                       own output embedding.  Initialising an output projection
                       from it is what Medusa does and is usually much better
                       than random.
    * ``shared_proj`` -- an ``nn.Linear(d_model, vocab, bias=False)`` already
                       initialised from ``lm_head_weight``.  Referencing this
                       one module from every block position costs its parameters
                       **once**; building your own projection per position costs
                       them once per position.  That is a real budget decision,
                       not a formality -- see "Parameter budget".  It is rebuilt
                       identically in both processes, so if you keep it FROZEN
                       you can hold it outside the returned module (e.g. in a
                       list attribute) and keep it out of the checkpoint.

``loss(module, hidden, tokens, aux) -> torch.Tensor``

    THE TRAINING OBJECTIVE -- return a scalar to be back-propagated.  The fixed
    driver calls it several times per optimiser step, on consecutive
    micro-batches, and accumulates the gradients; ``aux["n_micro"]`` says how
    many.  That is a memory decision on the harness's part and changes nothing
    about the objective: write ``loss`` as if it saw one batch.

    * ``hidden`` -- float32 ``(B, S, d_model)``, the FROZEN backbone's hidden
      state after each of ``S`` consecutive tokens.  Detached: no gradient flows
      into the backbone, which never trains.
    * ``tokens`` -- int64 ``(B, S + L)``.  ``tokens[b, t + k]`` is the token
      ``k`` positions after the one ``hidden[b, t]`` was produced by, so
      ``tokens[:, k : k + S]`` is the target sequence for block position ``k``.
    * ``aux``    -- dict with ``step``, ``total_steps``, ``n_micro`` and
      ``generator`` (a seeded ``torch.Generator``).  Draw any randomness your
      objective needs -- a diffusion noise level, a masking pattern -- from that
      generator, so the run stays a function of the seed.  It also carries the
      **target model's own opinion**, cached once by the harness:

        - ``aux["target_top"]``  -- int64 ``(B, S + L - 1, KD)``
        - ``aux["target_logp"]`` -- float32 ``(B, S + L - 1, KD)``

      ``target_top[b, p]`` are the target's ``KD`` most likely tokens for stream
      position ``p + 1``, with their log-probabilities, teacher-forced on the
      stream.  The training stream is made of the TARGET's own greedy answers to
      a set of training prompts (chat, code and math requests), so ``tokens``
      after a position are the target's greedy continuation of it.  For block position ``k`` (1-based) at hidden index ``t`` the
      relevant entry is ``[:, t + k - 1]``; the slice for a whole window is
      ``[:, k - 1 : k - 1 + S]``.

      Distilling from the full distribution rather than the argmax ``tokens``
      is what the EAGLE family of drafters does; training on ``tokens`` is what
      Medusa does.  Both are legitimate.

``propose(module, hidden) -> (cand_token, cand_logp, n_submit)``

    The block, from ONE backbone forward.  ``hidden`` is float32 ``(B,
    d_model)``: one vector per item, the backbone's hidden state at the position
    a decoding round starts from.  That is the entire input -- there are no
    tokens here, because at inference the continuation is exactly what is
    unknown.  It runs on the same device as training, in batches, and is called
    for every position a round could start from.

    Return
    * ``cand_token`` -- int ``(B, L, K)``, your ``K`` candidate vocabulary ids
      for each of the ``L`` block positions, **best first**.
    * ``cand_logp``  -- float ``(B, L, K)``, your log-probabilities for them.
      Recorded as a diagnostic; the metric does not read them.
    * ``n_submit``   -- int ``(B,)`` in ``[1, L]``, how many leading positions of
      the block you actually submit for verification.  Return ``L`` to submit
      the whole block.  Submitting fewer can only lower the accepted length, and
      pays off only when ``cfg["cost_c"] > 0``.

    No gradients, no model, no tokenizer, no target, no truth, and nothing about
    how you are scored.

Unlike the sibling `spec-*` tasks, whose child builds a fresh policy object per
item, **one object is built here and it persists across every evaluation item**,
because a trained head must.  Nothing is fed back between items -- no truth
enters this process and no score is returned -- so the most that persistence can
buy is transductive statistics over unlabelled features.

Parameter budget
----------------
Every trainable parameter of the module ``build`` returns is counted, and the
total is capped at 1.05x the largest baseline's.  Parameters shared between
block positions (``cfg["shared_proj"]``, or any module you reuse) are counted
once, because that is how ``nn.Module.parameters()`` counts them.  The cap is
generous -- Medusa's ``L - 1`` independent output projections set it -- so the
interesting designs are the ones that spend it on structure rather than on
copies of the vocabulary projection.

What is measured
----------------
``tau``, the tokens produced per decoding round -- the quantity Medusa, DFlash,
DFlash 2 and DSpark all report -- measured by decoding: the target's own greedy
answers to a set of held-out prompts are replayed round by round.  At a round
starting at position ``t`` let ``g_1, g_2, ...`` be the target's greedy
continuation.  The target verifies your submitted block in one forward and
accepts the longest prefix of ``g`` that your block's top-1 tokens match; that
same forward yields one more token for free, and the next round starts after it.

    tau     = (tokens produced) / (rounds),   k = the matching prefix within n_submit

and, where the setting prices verification,

    eff_tau = (tokens produced) / sum over rounds of (1 + cost_c * n_submit)

which is ``tau`` exactly when ``cost_c`` is 0.  Both are computed by a separate
process that holds the answers; this file never sees them.
"""
import numpy as np
import torch

def _distill(logits, aux, k, S):

        return total

    def propose(self, module, hidden):
        L, K = self.cfg["block_len"], self.cfg["top_k"]
        cost = float(self.cfg["cost_c"])
        B = hidden.shape[0]
        f = module.feats(hidden)
        toks, lps, cs = [], [], []
        prev = None
        for k in range(L):
            if k > 0:
                lg = module.proj(f[:, k]).float() + module.bias(prev).float()
                c = module.confidence(f[:, k], prev)
            else:
                # Position 1 carries NO intra-block dependency (there is no
                # previous token to condition on), so it is the frozen backbone's
                # own next-token distribution -- exactly what `default` and
                # `medusa` emit at position 1. Emitting the trained shared
                # projection here instead degrades position 1 below the frozen
                # lm_head, because that projection is pulled toward the harder
                # later positions under the fixed step budget; the effect is an
                # artefact of the budget, not of the Markov mechanism, and it is
                # sharpest at a larger vocabulary. The Markov transition bias and
                # the confidence schedule -- which ARE the method -- still act on
                # positions 2..L unchanged.
                lg = (hidden.float() @ self.cfg["lm_head_weight"].float().t())
                c = module.confidence(f[:, k], torch.zeros(B, dtype=torch.long,
                                                           device=hidden.device))
            lp = torch.log_softmax(lg, dim=-1)
            v, i = torch.topk(lp, K, dim=-1)
            prev = i[:, 0]                      # the token this position commits to
            toks.append(i)
            lps.append(v)
            cs.append(c)
        surv = torch.cumprod(torch.stack(cs, 1).clamp(0.0, 1.0), dim=1)  # (B, L)
        # Admit until the predicted throughput starts DECLINING (DSpark Sec. 3.3).
        # The LAST maximiser, not the first: when the cumulative survival
        # underflows to zero the throughput curve goes flat rather than down, and
        # a flat stretch costs nothing to keep -- at cost_c = 0 it is free, and
        # `argmax` would have stopped at the first plateau point and thrown away
        # positions the rule does not ask it to give up. (Caught pre-measurement
        # by the arm reporting n_submit 7.98 instead of 8.00 at cost_c = 0.)
        gain = torch.cumsum(surv, dim=1) + 1.0
        denom = 1.0 + cost * torch.arange(1, L + 1, device=surv.device).float()
        theta = gain / denom[None, :]
        best = theta.max(dim=1, keepdim=True).values
        pos = torch.arange(1, L + 1, device=surv.device).float()[None, :]
        n_submit = torch.where(theta >= best - 1e-9, pos, torch.zeros_like(pos))             .max(dim=1).values.cpu().numpy().astype(np.int64)
        return torch.stack(toks, 1), torch.stack(lps, 1), n_submit
